source.title: Hybrid Architectures for Language Models: Systematic Analysis and Design Insights
source.authors: Sangmin Bae; Bilge Acun; Haroun Habeeb; Seungyeon Kim; Chien-Yu Lin; Liang Luo; Jun-Jie Wang; Carole-Jean Wu

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through the appendices. Some plotted figure values are not represented in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines compute-optimal model-size and data allocations across architectures and compute budgets, using its own scaling experiments rather than reproducing the original scaling-law methods.
record.gate_note: The study directly reports compute-optimal scaling trends in §4.4 and Appendix M. Its NLL tables and other architecture comparisons are not recorded as power-law loss rows: the paper does not report a fit testing whether loss follows a power law or whether small-run fits predict larger runs. The downstream evaluations compare architectures, not downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: §4.4 and Appendix M run Chinchilla-style IsoFLOP sweeps: four sizes (100M–3B), five budgets (2e19–4e20 FLOPs), and quadratic fits per budget to find the loss-minimising size. The Transformer arm checks the Hoffmann token-to-parameter ratio. The Mamba and hybrid arms apply the same compute-optimal allocation question to new language-model architectures. The results bear directly on V3, and on V7 through architecture dependence of the optimal split.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it should add that Transformers favour ~20 tokens/param (as in Hoffmann) and Mamba favours larger models with less data. Hybrids lie in between, with intra-layer hybrids slightly more data-hungry. The authors present this as guidance for scaling hybrids, and conclude more broadly that hybrids beat homogeneous models in quality and efficiency.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains Transformer, Mamba, and hybrid models across compute budgets and derives compute-optimal scaling lines; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting and extrapolation procedure.

fits_no_version.finding: At roughly fixed parameter count (~1B) and 60B tokens, the choice of primitive, block ratio and Transformer-block position shifts DCLM NLL by up to ~0.05. Examples: Llama 2.750, intra-hybrid 2.712, single front Transformer block 2.771 vs middle 2.740 (Tables 5, 17, 20).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixing attention and SSM primitives, and where attention blocks sit, changes loss at fixed parameters and data more than Kaplan-style shape changes do.

record.problems: Scaling evidence is limited to models up to 3B parameters and compute budgets from 2e19 to 4e20 FLOPs. The compute-optimal trends are stated qualitatively, without numerical exponents or reported uncertainty.

untested.parts: NLL is reported across sizes and budgets (Tables 14–15), but no power-law fit in N, D or C is reported.
No extrapolation from small-run fits to larger runs.
No numerical exponents for N_opt or D_opt versus compute, and no test of their stability beyond 2e19–4e20 FLOPs and 3B parameters.
No depth/width shape sweep at fixed parameter count for Transformers.
No other modalities, repeated data or transfer scaling.
Downstream results compare architectures, not scale or loss trends.
No test of fitting method, parameter counting (non-embedding vs total) or schedule effects on exponents. Budgets reuse intermediate checkpoints of a trapezoid schedule, which is untested as a factor.

missing.what: Per-run IsoFLOP NLL values by size and budget, plus the loss-minimising size per budget, for all four architectures. Needed to read the compute-optimal points and ratio drift.
Fitted token-to-parameter ratios printed on the compute-optimal lines for each architecture (not in the extracted text).

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3. The Transformer arm reuses Hoffmann's IsoFLOP approach; the new contribution is applying it to Mamba and hybrids. Budgets were obtained by reusing intermediate checkpoints of the largest run with a trapezoid schedule. The scaling grid has only four sizes and parameter counts are non-embedding, so optima are coarse and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports NLL measurements across model sizes and compute budgets, but does not test whether loss follows a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute when the other quantities are not bottlenecks.
No test of predictions from power-law fits on small runs to substantially larger runs.
The study reports qualitative architecture-specific compute-optimal trends, but does not give numerical growth exponents or test their stability beyond the stated scales and budgets.
No controlled test isolating depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No scaling-law test in other modalities or training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream results compare architectures; the study does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.

The paper describes its fitting procedure but does not test whether exponents or optimal allocations change with fitting choices, parameter counting, schedules, or data, or whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Trained across compute budgets and used to identify compute-optimal model sizes and token allocations.
rows.value: Transformers favor a higher token-to-parameter ratio of around 20.
rows.note: The paper describes a compute-optimal line but does not report its numerical growth exponent.
rows.check: The authors state Transformers favour ~20 tokens/param, citing Hoffmann, which matches equal growth. No exponent or stability test is reported. Optima rest on a coarse 4-size grid. Raw Table 14 minima (1B at 8e19, 2e20, 4e20, i.e. ~11→55 tokens/param) suggest the ratio may drift, and the fitted Figure 5 ratios are not in the text. Value is correctly read; baseline should be 'Hoffmann ~20 tokens/param'.

source_check.correct: Observed for the reported qualitative compute-optimal allocation: Transformer favors approximately 20 tokens per parameter. Numerical allocation exponents and their stability are untested, rather than demonstrated to be partial.
source_check.locator_found: §4.4; Table 4 right-panel caption; Appendix M; Figure 5 caption; Table 14.
source_check.problem: The partial state confuses limited quantification with an observed incomplete effect.

rows.subject: Mamba
rows.operation_detail: Trained across compute budgets and used to identify compute-optimal model sizes and token allocations.
rows.value: Mamba performs best with larger models and less data feeding.
rows.note: The paper describes a compute-optimal line but does not report its numerical growth exponent.
rows.check: For V3, a compute-optimal line exists, but Mamba's split favours larger models and fewer tokens than the Transformer, e.g. at 4e20 the 3B model (2.691) beats 1B (2.712), ~7 tokens/param. For V7 the state is observed: the optimal split depends on architecture. No exponents are reported.

source_check.correct: Observed for qualitative compute-optimal scaling and V7 architecture dependence: Mamba favors larger models and less data than Transformer. Numerical allocation exponents and stability are untested.
source_check.problem: A single partial state misrepresents the observed architecture-dependent allocation, especially for V7.

rows.subject: Inter-layer hybrid
rows.operation_detail: Trained across compute budgets and used to identify compute-optimal model sizes and token allocations.
rows.value: Hybrid models show intermediate scaling behavior between Transformer and Mamba.
rows.note: The paper describes a compute-optimal line but does not report its numerical growth exponent.
rows.check: Optimal allocation lies between Transformer and Mamba (stated qualitatively; Table 15 values not rowed). This bears on V7 as an architecture-dependent split, where the state is observed. Block ratio 1:5.

source_check.correct: Observed for qualitative compute-optimal scaling and V7 architecture dependence: inter-layer hybrid allocation lies between Transformer and Mamba. Numerical allocation exponents and stability are untested.
source_check.locator_found: §4.4; Table 4 right-panel caption; Appendix M; Table 15.
source_check.problem: The reported intermediate allocation is observed; missing numerical exponents do not establish a partial effect.

rows.subject: Intra-layer hybrid
rows.operation_detail: Trained across compute budgets and used to identify compute-optimal model sizes and token allocations.
rows.value: Hybrid models show intermediate scaling behavior, with intra-layer hybrids being a little more data-hungry.
rows.note: The paper describes a compute-optimal line but does not report its numerical growth exponent.
rows.check: Optimal allocation is intermediate and slightly more data-hungry than the inter-layer hybrid. Qualitative only; for V7 the state is observed. Note: the Figure 5 panel (d) caption mislabels it 'Inter-layer hybrid'.

source_check.correct: Observed for qualitative compute-optimal scaling and V7 architecture dependence: intra-layer hybrids have intermediate allocation and are slightly more data-hungry than inter-layer hybrids. Numerical allocation exponents and stability are untested.
source_check.problem: The partial state does not fit the observed qualitative architecture dependence.

relationships.reason: The authors report a compute-optimal ratio of ~20 tokens/param, matching Hoffmann's equal scaling (r1). The result is qualitative, with no exponent, and rests on a coarse grid.
relationships.display_finding: The coarse experimental grid indicated an optimal ratio near 20 tokens per parameter.

relationships.condition: Mamba 2 and 1:5 inter-/intra-layer hybrid language models, same grid
relationships.reason: The compute-optimal split shifts with architecture: Mamba prefers larger models and less data, hybrids fall in between (r2–r4). A single allocation rule does not carry across architectures.
relationships.display_finding: Mamba 2 favored larger models and less data, while inter-layer and intra-layer hybrids lay between Mamba and Transformer allocations.
